Water quality in the Millbrook catchment has been recorded by volunteers since the county survey of 1994, when nitrate levels were first logged at eleven sites along the main channel and its two tributaries. The early sheets are patchy: samples were taken whenever somebody had a free afternoon, and the glass electrodes were not always calibrated properly before use. Even so the series is long enough to be useful, and the district council has continued to pay for the monthly visits. Each site is walked on the first Saturday of the month, whatever the weather, and the readings are typed into a shared spreadsheet by the following Tuesday, though a handful of winter entries arrive late.

The upper reaches are shallow and quick, running over gravel between alder roots, and the water there is cold even in August. Below the old mill the channel widens, the current slows, and fine sediment settles on the stones. Two sewage works discharge into this lower stretch, one above the weir and one below it, and the outflow pipes are easy to find because the banks around them stay green all winter. A footbridge crosses just downstream of the second outfall, and the sampling point sits a few metres beyond the bridge, where the river turns north toward the estuary and the tide begins to show in the water.

The stretch below the mill has changed hands twice since the survey began. A gravel company held the fishing rights for most of the nineties and dredged the channel each autumn, which the older volunteers still complain about when the subject comes up. The angling club bought the rights in 2001 and stopped the dredging almost at once, though it took several seasons for the bed to settle. Fencing went up along the eastern bank in 2004, keeping cattle out of the water, and a strip of willow and alder was planted behind it the same year. Most of those trees were no more than cuttings when they went in, and the bank behind them was bare mud for two summers.

Over the past twenty years the nitrate concentration at the lower sites has fallen steadily, from a mean of almost nine milligrams per litre in the late nineties to just under four today, and the invertebrate counts have more than doubled over the same period. The improvement is not uniform. Readings taken after heavy rain still spike for a day or two, and the spring floods have become more erratic, arriving earlier and lasting longer than they did in the first decade of the record. Volunteers have grown used to rewriting their schedules around them, and the May visits are now often made in waders rather than boots.

Not everything in the record can be explained by the management changes, and the volunteers are careful to say so in the annual report. Some of the fall in nitrate may simply reflect the closure of two dairy farms further up the valley in 2008 and 2010, and the weather has been kind to the river for much of the period. The report also notes that sampling effort has been uneven, with gaps of several months after the foot and mouth restrictions, and that the laboratory changed method in 2013. The council has asked for a proper statistical review before any targets are set, and the angling club has offered to pay for it.

The full dataset, including the original survey sheets, the calibration logs and the photographs taken at each site, is held at the council offices and can be consulted on request. A summary is published every March.
